stories.summary: Logo is a Lisp dialect programming language designed as an educational tool, featuring interactive interpreted execution with immediate feedback to aid learning and debugging. Its key strengths include modularity through small procedures, extensibility that allows users to build complex programs incrementally, and flexible data typing that simplifies programming compared to stricter languages. Some enhanced versions add features like object-oriented programming, multi-tasking, and massive parallelism for more advanced applications.

stories.summary: This article provides an interactive guide to the Spanning Tree Protocol (STP), explaining how it prevents network loops by selectively blocking cables to create a loop-free tree structure in Ethernet networks. Through browser-based simulations running a real RSTP implementation, readers can visualize how the protocol elects a root bridge, assigns port roles, and recovers from cable failures in under a second. The guide covers the protocol's evolution from the 1980s to modern RSTP and MSTP variants, along with detailed explanations of its complex state machine and mechanisms.

topComments.author: stego-tech
topComments.text: Counter-argument: bullshit jobs are beneficial to the wider economy. Society demands consumption, which is funded via wages. The higher consumption, the more the economy grows. Ergo, having more people employed with higher wages creates more economic activity, which in turn fuels more growth, which fuels more jobs, etc. While eliminating bullshit jobs sounds great on its own merits, eliminating the wages for said jobs can actually clog the local engine by lowering wages, raising unemployment, slowing hiring, and curtailing growth. If 15% of jobs are “bullshit” to be eliminated, that’s a 15% reduction in SaaS and seat-based revenues, which means those companies providing services have to cut their headcount, which startles others…you get the idea. I suggest that instead of cutting “bullshit jobs”, we instead reduce working hours across the board (and penalize overtime) such that more folks have an opportunity to engage in meaningful and valuable labor in exchange for higher wages. Rather than burning out a smaller portion of folks with longer hours, we share the load across multiple folks over a shorter time frame. The extra downtime creates more opportunity for economic activity, which in turn will grow the economy.

stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I maintain a Java library and want to add a facility for user-defined extensions to a class, so that users of that class can attach extensions of their choice to any instance of that class. The library itself just stores these extensions, but does not evaluate their content. One design idea that I came across suggested storing these extensions in a Map<Class<?>, Object> type. This provides two benefits: Users can use any class of their choice as an extension, no need for the extension to be a subclass of a particular class or implement a particular interface. Users can store multiple extensions in an instance. (As long as each extension is of a different class – else wrap instances of the same class in a collection type.) The * extension class will always correspond to its key. */ return (T) extensions.get(clazz); } public boolean hasExtension(Class<?> clazz) { return extensions.containsKey(clazz); } public void setExtension(Object extension) { extensions.put(extension.getClass(), extension); } // TODO methods to enumerate/iterate over extensions, clear all extensions However, this has one potentially undesirable side effect. stackOverflowQuestions.title: Port Type Handling and Validation for APIs
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I want to clarify an issue I’m facing with the port type handling. Currently, we have multiple port types, and the same API may need to fetch records based on different port types. I’m thinking of defining the supported port types in appsettings.json as a base configuration. The main requirement is: The frontend should be able to pass the portType when it is required. The API should validate whether the passed portType is actually supported/configured. For APIs where portType is not required, the frontend should not have to send it. I don’t think we should put this validation in middleware because not every request needs a portType . Doing it globally in middleware could create unnecessary issues for APIs that don’t use port types. In Swagger/API testing, I should also be able to pass the portType explicitly so I can test the same API with multiple port types. Ideally, the available port types should come from the base configuration ( appsettings.json ) rather than being hardcoded in multiple places. For example, if one API can return records for PortTypeA , PortTypeB , and PortTypeC , I should be able to call the same API with the required port type and have the API validate it against the configured values. Could we handle this at the API/controller/service level, or through a reusable validation mechanism, instead of putting it in global middleware? The goal is to have one consistent approach that works for both the frontend and Swagger testing, while allowing APIs that don’t require a port type to continue working normally.
